It occurs 64 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Numbers, where instructions for these offerings are especially concentrated.

This word occurs three times in the Old Testament, all within Jeremiah 38:11–12. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary lexical sense is the object called “clouts.”

The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Proverbs, at Proverbs 11:3 and Proverbs 15:4. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the same: perverseness as a recognizable moral quality.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Ephlal.” It refers to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The surrounding evidence identifies its role within a birth or begetting sequence, so the name belongs to a recorded family line. Its precise significance as a name is not explained beyond this genealogical use.

Parshandatha is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 9:7, and the English rendering preserves it as “Parshandatha.” The available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain its meaning as a name. This Hebrew word means “thirsty.” It describes someone experiencing a need for water. In the Old Testament, it is used of people who lack refreshment and of thirst as a recognizable human condition. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Bible, appearing from Deuteronomy through Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains the condition of being thirsty.

e.h: A Hebrew Measure Called a Cab
e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “cab,” a measured item named in the Old Testament. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible, at 2 Kings 6:25, so its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context. The word functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. Its single occurrence makes it a rare biblical term, but its basic reference is clear from its rendering as “cab.”

This Hebrew word means “fever,” naming a condition of intense bodily heat or illness. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, in Leviticus 26:16 and Deuteronomy 28:22. In both passages, it belongs to a list of afflictions described as consequences that may come upon Israel. The word itself identifies the sickness, while the surrounding passage explains its place among other troubles. Its basic sense remains a physical fever rather than a general description of distress or hardship.

e.t: “Kohath” is a personal name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a man in Israel’s genealogical records and, by extension, the family descended from him. The name occurs 32 times, from Genesis through First Chronicles, with especially frequent appearances in Numbers and First Chronicles. It is therefore not a general description or action word, but a proper name marking a particular ancestral line.

Keros is a Hebrew name preserved in English transliteration rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra 2:44 and once in Nehemiah 7:47. Since both occurrences render it as “Keros,” its meaning is best understood as the identity of a person or family named Keros, while the available information does not establish a further lexical definition or explain the surrounding list context.

Its basic meaning remains the same in both passages: a chain that can be given to or placed on someone. The surrounding verse determines the particular scene, but the word itself names the chain.

This Hebrew verb describes becoming “thin” or being “famished,” expressing a state of reduced bodily fullness or nourishment. It appears twice in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 17:4 and Zephaniah 2:11. This Hebrew word means “joy.” It functions as the word that expresses or identifies joy in a sentence, rather than naming a person or place. This Hebrew word means “errors,” referring to mistakes or wrong actions. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 19:12. Its central idea remains clear: it identifies errors—things a person may fail to recognize or may need to have brought to light. The word therefore points to human wrongdoing or fault without, by itself, explaining the particular kind involved.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “blue,” referring to a blue-colored material or textile. It is used 49 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Exodus, where blue is associated with the making of the tabernacle, its coverings, and priestly garments. The word also appears in commands concerning the construction and presentation of these sacred items, showing its practical role as a specified material or color in worship furnishings and clothing. Its broader use extends beyond Exodus into other Old Testament books.
